lead: Infotainment traffic is different from control traffic: audio and video must flow without a break, at megabits per second, between the head unit, amplifier, navigation, phone and displays. MOST (Media Oriented Systems Transport) was built for this. It is a ring, usually of plastic optical fibre, in which a timing master sends frames at the audio sample rate and every device takes its stream out of the frame and puts its own in. The ring is joined to the car's CAN, LIN and FlexRay buses by a gateway. This chapter explains MOST, the ways networks are coupled and what a central gateway does, with channel and delay numbers worked out.
prereq: You need the ring topology and OSI layers from topology, OSI model and classification, and the CAN frame time from CAN and CAN FD.

sections.h3: MOST: a synchronous ring for media

blocks.text: In a MOST network up to 64 devices are joined in a ring: each device receives from the one before and sends to the one after. MOST25 uses plastic optical fibre (POF) with a 1 mm core and a red LED: light, cheap and immune to electrical noise. MOST50 and MOST150 can also run on copper wires.

One device, usually the head unit, is the timing master. It sends frames round the ring without a pause at the system frequency, 44.1 kHz (the CD sample rate) or 48 kHz. Every other device is a timing slave: it recovers the clock from the arriving frames, takes the bytes meant for it, puts its own bytes into the free places and passes the frame on. Because every device runs on the master's clock, audio arrives one sample per frame with no buffering and no lost samples.

At the application layer each device is described by function blocks (for example an amplifier block or a tuner block) that other devices control with short control messages. Because the ring passes through every device, one broken fibre or one dead device stops the whole ring; MOST therefore has a ring break diagnosis that finds the position of the break, and the gateway reports it to the workshop tester.

sections.h3: The MOST25 frame and its three channels

blocks.text: A MOST25 frame is 64 bytes (512 bits): 1 byte of header (preamble and boundary descriptor), 60 bytes of data, 2 bytes of control data and 1 byte of trailer (frame control and parity). The 60 data bytes are split, by the boundary descriptor, between two channels:

items: Synchronous channel: byte positions reserved for one stream for as long as it plays. A 16-bit stereo audio stream sends one sample of each side per frame, so it needs 4 bytes in every frame.
Asynchronous channel: the rest of the 60 bytes, shared by packet data such as map tiles, address books and pictures, which can wait a little.
Control channel: the 2 control bytes of each frame. A control message is spread over a block of 16 frames, and the channel carries commands ("amplifier, volume up"), status and network management.

blocks.where: R is the data rate of a channel in bit/s; f is the frame rate, equal to the system frequency (44 100 frames per second at 44.1 kHz). The whole 64-byte frame gives 64 × 8 × 44 100 = 22.58 Mbit/s, often quoted as about 23 Mbit/s for MOST25.

blocks.text: MOST50 doubles the frame to 1024 bits and MOST150 makes it 3072 bits, about 150 Mbit/s at 48 kHz; MOST150 also adds a channel that carries Ethernet packets and one for isochronous video. Many new cars now use Ethernet with AVB/TSN for media instead.

sections.h3: Coupling networks: repeaters, bridges, routers and gateways

blocks.text: Two networks can be joined at different OSI layers. A repeater (layer 1) only regenerates the signal, so both sides are one network. A bridge (layer 2) joins two segments of the same protocol and passes only frames that must cross. A router (layer 3) chooses a path between networks by address. A gateway works up to layer 7 and joins networks with different protocols, rates and frame formats. In a car, the buses are of different kinds, so they are coupled through gateways, most often one central gateway with a port on every domain bus.
The central gateway does six jobs:

items: Message routing: a routing table says which identifiers received on one bus are sent on which other buses; the rest are dropped.
Signal routing: it unpacks signals from incoming frames and packs them into new frames for the other bus, for example engine speed and coolant temperature into one body-bus frame for the cluster.
Rate adaptation: it buffers frames between a 500 kbit/s bus and a 125 kbit/s bus, or between CAN and MOST, and may send a fast-changing signal less often on the slow side.
Filtering and protection: it blocks frames that must not cross, so the infotainment side can never send a brake or steering message.
Diagnostic routing: the OBD socket is wired to the gateway, which passes the tester's requests to every ECU on every bus.
Network management: it wakes the buses when a door opens or a key is used and lets them sleep when the car is parked.

blocks.text: A networked car of today is an example: a 500 kbit/s powertrain CAN (engine, gearbox), a chassis CAN or FlexRay (ABS and ESP, steering, suspension), a 125 kbit/s body CAN with LIN sub-buses (doors, seats, climate), a MOST ring or Ethernet for infotainment, and the OBD socket, all meeting at the gateway. A frame that crosses waits for its turn in the gateway, so the delay of a crossing message is the sum of its frame time on the input bus, the gateway's processing time, any wait for the output bus and its frame time on the output bus.

examples.question: A MOST25 ring runs at 44.1 kHz. The head unit plays a 16-bit stereo radio stream to the amplifier, and the DVD player sends 6-channel 16-bit surround sound. (a) What is the rate of one stereo stream and how many bytes per frame does it need? (b) How many bytes do the two streams use, and what asynchronous rate is left in the 60 data bytes? (c) How many stereo streams could the frame carry at most? (d) What is the control channel rate?
steps: (a) Stereo rate = 44 100 samples/s × 16 bits × 2 sides = 1 411 200 bit/s = 1.41 Mbit/s. Per frame: 2 sides × 16 bits = 32 bits = 4 bytes.
(b) Surround: 6 channels × 2 bytes = 12 bytes per frame. Both streams: 4 + 12 = 16 synchronous bytes.
Bytes left for the asynchronous channel: 60 − 16 = 44 bytes. Rate = 44 × 8 × 44 100 = 15 523 200 bit/s ≈ 15.5 Mbit/s.
(c) Most stereo streams: 60 ÷ 4 = 15 if every data byte were synchronous.
examples.answer: (a) 1.41 Mbit/s, 4 bytes per frame; (b) 16 bytes used, about 15.5 Mbit/s left for packet data; (c) 15 stereo streams at most; (d) 705.6 kbit/s for control.

examples.question: The central gateway forwards a standard 8-data-byte frame (111 bits with the interframe space, no stuffing) from the 500 kbit/s powertrain CAN to the 125 kbit/s body CAN. Its processing takes 0.20 ms and the body bus is free. (a) Find the delay from the start of the frame on the powertrain bus to the end of its copy on the body bus. (b) The gateway forwards 10 such frames every 20 ms. What load do they put on the body bus?
steps: Input frame time: 111 bits ÷ 500 000 bit/s = 0.000222 s = 0.222 ms.
Output frame time: 111 bits ÷ 125 000 bit/s = 0.000888 s = 0.888 ms.
Bits per second on the body bus: 10 × 111 bits ÷ 0.020 s = 1110 ÷ 0.020 = 55 500 bit/s.
Load: 55 500 ÷ 125 000 = 0.444, that is 44.4 per cent of the body bus from forwarded frames alone.
examples.answer: (a) 1.31 ms; (b) 44.4 per cent, so the gateway must forward only the frames the body bus really needs, or send them less often.

traps: MOST is not arbitrated like CAN. Synchronous streams own fixed byte positions in every frame; only the asynchronous and control channels are shared.
One broken fibre stops the whole MOST ring, not just the next device; this is why the ring break diagnosis exists.
A gateway is not a repeater or a bridge: it translates between different protocols and decides which signals cross, up to OSI layer 7.
Forwarding is not free: the crossing message pays its frame time on both buses plus the gateway's processing, and the slow bus pays its load.
The MOST frame rate equals the audio sample rate (44.1 or 48 kHz), so a stream uses bytes per frame, not bits per second, in the frame budget.

quiz.q: What do the letters MOST stand for, and what topology and medium does MOST25 use?
quiz.a: Media Oriented Systems Transport. A ring of up to 64 devices on plastic optical fibre with a red LED.

quiz.q: What does the timing master do in a MOST ring?
quiz.a: It sends frames continuously at the system frequency (44.1 or 48 kHz). The other devices recover their clock from these frames, so every stream is in step with one clock.

quiz.q: A mono 16-bit navigation voice stream runs on MOST25 at 44.1 kHz. How many bytes per frame and what rate does it use?
quiz.a: One 16-bit sample per frame = 2 bytes. Rate = 2 × 8 × 44 100 = 705.6 kbit/s.

quiz.q: A gateway forwards a 111-bit frame from 500 kbit/s CAN to 250 kbit/s CAN with 0.1 ms processing. Find the delay.
Explain the difference between a bridge and a gateway.
quiz.a: A bridge joins two segments of the same protocol at layer 2 and passes frames unchanged. A gateway joins different protocols, rates and formats, and can unpack, repack, filter and re-time signals up to layer 7.

quiz.q: Why should the gateway block messages from the infotainment bus to the chassis bus?
quiz.a: The infotainment side runs large software and is connected to phones, USB and the internet, so it is the easiest part to attack or to crash. If it could send chassis frames, a fault or attacker there could command brakes or steering. Filtering keeps safety domains separate.

beyond: Not for the exam. Gateways are turning into central computers or zone controllers with Ethernet backbones, and media links are moving from MOST to Ethernet AVB/TSN. Search for central gateway ECU, AVB audio and AUTOSAR PDU router.
